# Economics — Theories of the Business Cycle — Interpretive Methodology Guide

> **Purpose:** Guide interpretation of literature on business cycles, crises, and
> especially *financial/monetary* theories of the cycle — mapping each tradition's
> methodological commitments, philosophy-of-science provenance, genealogy, and the
> conflicts that shape the field.
> **Applies to:** financial theory of business cycles; monetary theory of the cycle;
> credit cycles; theories of crises, fluctuations, and economic instability.
> **Relationship:** Reasoning reference, **NOT authoritative**; one interpretation among
> several. Not a citation database — citation keys below are *pointers* and must be
> resolved and verified per project against `Projects/*/references/bibliography.bib` by
> `@reference-manager`.
> **Authority Position:** Complements `orchestrator.agent.md`; does not supersede.
> **Commissioned by:** `@interpretation-advisor` · **Authored by:** `@content-enricher`
> · **Maintenance owner:** `@agent-updater`
> **Audited by:** `@reference-manager` (existence) + `@technical-validator` (claim ledger)
> + `@adversarial` (selection) + `@conflict-auditor` (contradictions/boundary)
> **Epistemic Status:** interpretation, contested.
> **status:** provisional
> **Last audited:** not yet — shipped as a worked exemplar pending the full audit chain.

## Surveys the tradition superset was drawn from

This superset is **not neutral**. It is drawn from, and inherits the canon and blind
spots of:

- **Schumpeter, *History of Economic Analysis* (1954)** — comprehensive but reflects
  Schumpeter's own vantage; strong on continental and Austrian thought, lighter on later
  formal macro (it predates it).
- **Blaug, *Economic Theory in Retrospect* (5th ed., 1997)** — Anglophone,
  rational-reconstruction bias; strong on classical/neoclassical logic, thinner on
  Marxian and heterodox institutional cycle theory.
- **Screpanti & Zamagni, *An Outline of the History of Economic Thought* (2005)** — added
  to widen coverage of Marxian and heterodox positions that the first two under-weight.

**Known exclusions inherited from these surveys:** non-Western monetary thought;
much post-Keynesian and structuralist/dependency cycle theory; ecological-economics
framings of instability. A project touching those should commission a superset extension.

## Traditions / Schools

| School | Core methodological commitment | Philosophy-of-science source | Key figures | Canonical texts (pointer keys) | Standard of evidence |
|--------|-------------------------------|------------------------------|-------------|-------------------------------|----------------------|
| **Austrian (monetary over-investment)** | Methodological individualism; subjectivism; verbal causal-genetic theory; deep-capital structure | Praxeology / apriorism — theory as deductive from the action axiom (Mises); *Verstehen* | Menger, Böhm-Bawerk, Wicksell (bridge), Mises, Hayek | `Menger1871`, `BohmBawerk1889`, `Wicksell1898`, `Mises1912`, `Hayek1931`, `Mises1949` | Logical derivation from premises; historical illustration, not statistical test |
| **Keynesian** | Aggregate/macro reasoning; fundamental (non-probabilistic) uncertainty; effective demand | Keynes's own theory of probability & uncertainty; holism over microfoundations | Keynes; later Kalecki (independently) | `Keynes1930`, `Keynes1936`, `KeynesTP1921` | Aggregate relationships; expectations & conventions; less reliance on equilibrium |
| **Monetarist** | Quantity theory; stable money-demand; money as dominant cyclical driver | Friedman's instrumentalist positivism — judge theories by predictive success, not realism of assumptions | Friedman, Schwartz | `Friedman1953`, `FriedmanSchwartz1963` | Predictive success against time-series evidence |
| **New Classical / Real Business Cycle** | Walrasian general equilibrium *always*; rational expectations; microfounded, quantitative DSGE | Formalist/axiomatic modelling; equilibrium method; econometric calibration | Lucas, Kydland, Prescott | `Lucas1972`, `Lucas1976`, `KydlandPrescott1982` | Internal consistency + quantitative match of a calibrated model to moments of data |
| **Minskyan / financial-instability** | Endogenous financial fragility; balance-sheet & debt dynamics; institutions matter | Post-Keynesian; Keynes's uncertainty + institutional/financial detail | Minsky | `Minsky1986`, `Minsky1992` | Institutional-historical pattern of financing regimes (hedge→speculative→Ponzi) |
| **Marxian** | Historical materialism; crises endogenous to capitalist accumulation | Dialectical method; labour theory of value | Marx; later Marxian crisis theorists | `MarxCapital1867`, `MarxCapital3` | Structural/dialectical argument; tendencies, not point predictions |

## Genealogy (lineage to foundational figures)

> Each arrow is either attributed to a named secondary source **as that source's claim**,
> or marked `[editors' inference — unsourced]`. None is asserted as settled fact.

**Money, interest, and the critique of unlimited acquisition — back to Aristotle**
- Aristotle distinguishes *oikonomia* (household provisioning) from *chrematistike*
  (unlimited money-making), and treats interest/usury as "unnatural" — *Politics* I.8–10;
  money as a measure and medium — *Nicomachean Ethics* V.5. (per `Aristotle-Politics`,
  `Aristotle-NE`; and Meikle, *Aristotle's Economic Thought* 1995, `Meikle1995`).
- Aristotle's analysis of the exchange-value/money form → **Marx's** M–C–M′ circuit and
  his treatment of the money-form: *Marx explicitly quotes and credits Aristotle* in
  *Capital* vol. I, ch. 1–3 and ch. 5. (per `MarxCapital1867`; discussed in `Meikle1995`).
- Aristotelian/Scholastic interest doctrine → the classical and then **Böhm-Bawerk's**
  theory of interest: Böhm-Bawerk surveys and critiques the prior "exploitation" and
  "abstinence" interest theories before advancing his own agio (time-preference/
  roundaboutness) theory — *Capital and Interest* (1884/1889). (per `BohmBawerk1889`
  [*History and Critique of Interest Theories*]; and Schumpeter 1954, `Schumpeter1954`).

**The monetary/financial cycle line**
- **Wicksell** (1898) develops the *cumulative process*: divergence of the *market* rate
  of interest from the *natural* rate drives cumulative price movement. (per `Wicksell1898`).
- Wicksell's natural-vs-market-rate → **Mises (1912)** and **Hayek (1931)** monetary
  over-investment / Austrian business-cycle theory: credit expansion pushes the loan rate
  below the natural rate, distorting the intertemporal capital structure. *That Wicksell's
  cumulative-process framework is the proximate antecedent of the Austrian cycle theory* is
  a standard historiographical reading. (per `Schumpeter1954`; and Blaug 1997, `Blaug1997`).
- Böhm-Bawerk's capital theory (roundaboutness, period of production) → Hayek's
  capital-structure ("Hayekian triangle") account of the cycle. (per `Blaug1997`;
  Hayek 1931, `Hayek1931`).
- **Keynes**'s *Treatise on Money* (1930) also builds on Wicksell's natural-rate framing
  before the *General Theory* (1936) breaks toward effective demand and liquidity
  preference. (per `Schumpeter1954`; `Keynes1930`, `Keynes1936`).
- **Minsky** extends Keynes's uncertainty and the financial detail of the *Treatise* into
  an endogenous financial-instability hypothesis. (per `Minsky1992`, which states its own
  Keynesian lineage).

**Method-genealogy inferences (lower confidence)**
- Mises's apriorist praxeology → a broadly Kantian conception of synthetic a priori
  knowledge `[editors' inference — unsourced]` — frequently asserted, but the exact
  Kant→Mises dependency is contested and must be sourced before use.
- A direct doctrinal line from Scholastic just-price/usury analysis to modern monetary
  cycle theory `[editors' inference — unsourced]` — plausible but not established here.

## Interpretive nuances (the same word, different meanings)

| Term | Austrian | Keynesian / Minskyan | New Classical / RBC |
|------|----------|----------------------|---------------------|
| **Equilibrium** | A tendency / coordination state rarely reached; disequilibrium is where the action is | A resting point that can be a *persistent under-employment* state | A state the economy is *always in*; fluctuations are optimal responses to shocks |
| **Capital** | Heterogeneous, time-structured production stages | A homogeneous fund / `K` in an aggregate function | Aggregate `K`, calibrated |
| **Uncertainty** | Radical, but handled via entrepreneurship | *Fundamental / non-ergodic* — not reducible to probability (Keynes, Minsky) | Reducible to known probability distributions (rational expectations) |
| **"Natural" rate of interest** | Intertemporal-coordination rate (Wicksell→Mises/Hayek) | Framing Keynes ultimately subordinates to liquidity preference | Often a model-implied real rate |

## Conflicts register

| Conflict | Kind | Stakes | Provenance of each side's commitment |
|----------|------|--------|--------------------------------------|
| **Methodenstreit** (1880s) | methodological | Is economic knowledge deductive theory or historical induction? | Menger's theory-first method vs Schmoller's Historical School. (per `Schumpeter1954`, `Blaug1997`) — set the Austrian commitment to theory over historicism |
| **Socialist calculation debate** (1920s–40s) | intellectual/political | Can a planned economy rationally allocate without market prices? | Mises/Hayek (prices as knowledge) vs Lange/Lerner (market socialism). (per Lavoie, `Lavoie1985`) — deepened the Austrian emphasis on dispersed knowledge & the price system |
| **Keynes–Hayek** (1930s) | intellectual | Cause of, and cure for, the slump: over-investment vs deficient demand | *Prices and Production* vs *Treatise/General Theory*; LSE vs Cambridge. (per Caldwell's introductions in Hayek's *Collected Works*, `Caldwell1995`) |
| **Formalist revolution** (1950s) | methodological | Mathematization & axiomatization of economics | Samuelson/Debreu formalism reshaping what counts as "theory". (per Blaug, "The Formalist Revolution of the 1950s", `Blaug2003`) — marginalizes verbal Austrian & institutional method |
| **Monetarist counter-revolution / Lucas critique** (1960s–70s) | intellectual | Microfoundations, rational expectations, policy ineffectiveness | Friedman, then Lucas, vs Keynesian macro. (per `Lucas1976`; Johnson, `Johnson1971`) |

## Interpretive directives (how the team should read this domain's sources)

1. **Attribute claims to each school's own standard of evidence.** Do not fault an
   Austrian text for lacking econometrics, or an RBC paper for not being "realistic" —
   each answers to a different bar (see the nuances table).
2. **Disambiguate load-bearing terms** ("equilibrium", "capital", "natural rate",
   "uncertainty") *per school* before comparing claims.
3. **Trace a claim's methodological provenance** before adjudicating a dispute — many
   business-cycle disagreements are downstream of the Methodenstreit and the formalist
   revolution, not of the data.
4. **Keep genealogy claims sourced-or-flagged** — carry the `(per …)` / `[editors'
   inference]` tags into any Interpretive Map Brief; never upgrade an inference to a fact.
